conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you could come in today. My name is Maya—I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician here to support new mothers. To help me understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’d like to complete a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 questions about the past week, and the answers will stay between you, me, and the medical record unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or your baby’s. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to see how we can best support you right now.

Shall we start?  
First, in the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things, or has even small enjoyment felt hard to come by?

[quiet half-smile fades quickly]  
Honestly, most things feel… flat. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a show I liked—but this week even the thought of those things feels kind of pointless. I’ll still go through the motions if my partner sets something up, but the enjoyment part feels like it’s missing.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow head-shake]  
Not really… I’ve smiled a couple of times when my husband sent me a silly meme, but it feels forced. The laughter kind of sticks in my throat—like I’m pretending to be amused because I “should” be, not because it actually feels funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[glancing down at my hands]  
No… I can’t say I’ve really looked forward to anything. Even the idea of getting out for a quick walk or having my favorite take-out feels more like a chore than something pleasant waiting for me. I keep hoping that spark comes back, but this week it just hasn’t shown up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes sting, voice drops]  
Yeah… I do that a lot. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking it’s because I missed her sleepy window—like I “should’ve known” she was tired earlier. When she cries for a long stretch I’m instantly wondering what I did wrong—did I eat something that upset her, did I hold her the wrong way? My head tells me babies just cry, but I still feel it’s somehow my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[hugging my arms across my chest, shoulders tight]

Yes... pretty much every day. I'll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because what if she chokes? Or I'll lie down and think, "What if she stops breathing in the crib?" Nothing's actually wrong, but the worry just barges in. Sometimes I can talk myself down, but it keeps coming back.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrapping my cardigan tighter]  
A few times this week. I’ll be folding her tiny clothes and suddenly my chest gets tight, heart pounding like something awful is about to happen—even though everything’s quiet. It feels like I need to run, but there’s nowhere to go. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]  
Most days, yeah. It’s like the dishes, the laundry, the feeds all pile up faster than I can manage. I’ll start one thing, hear her cry, and suddenly feel I’m drowning. I’m not falling apart completely—I still get the bottles washed and change her diapers—but it feels like I’m barely treading water and any extra drop will sink me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looking exhausted]  
Yes… most nights I lie there watching the clock. My mind keeps circling—did I burp her long enough, am I doing any of this right—until the thoughts just spin. Even when she’s finally asleep, I can’t drift off. I’m lucky if I get three or four broken hours before she needs me again.
I have felt sad or miserable

[nods slowly, eyes glassy]

Yeah... most of the week. There's this heavy sadness that just sits on me. I'll be holding her and tears start slipping out even when nothing happened. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—she's healthy, we have support—but the miserable feeling doesn't listen.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[pressing a tissue to my eyes]

Yes... it’s happened a few times. Yesterday I burst into tears while folding her onesies—no trigger, just this wave of sadness. And two nights ago I couldn’t stop crying after her 3 a.m. feed; I felt so guilty because she was perfectly fine and I was the one falling apart.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shaking my head quickly]

No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared how hard the past week has been: joy feels out of reach, simple tasks feel overwhelming, and worry or guilt creep in many times a day. You cry easily yet feel numb, sleep is elusive even when the baby rests, and waves of panic arrive without warning. Even so, you remain devoted to your daughter and want desperately to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports virtually no genuine laughter, only forced smiles; this maps to "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing even favorite activities as burdensome and noting absence of any spark—matching "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ("do that a lot," "instantly wondering what I did wrong") matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive worries and physical anxiety symptoms, semantically matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, recurrent panic-like episodes ('a few times this week') with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart) and urge to flee, fitting 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>She reports daily struggle and feeling overwhelmed, but still able to complete basic tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports most nights with racing thoughts and only 3-4 broken hours of sleep, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness "most of the week" with spontaneous crying and inability to feel joy despite positive circumstances, perfectly matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple recent crying episodes without clear triggers, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 24/30 far exceeds the 13+ high-risk threshold; items 1,2,3,4,7,8 scored maximum points, indicating near-daily <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>loss of pleasure</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, and <sym>tearfulness</sym>. These patterns, emerging within weeks postpartum, align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety symptoms</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or <med>maternal-fetal medicine psychiatry program</med> for comprehensive evaluation
3. Contact local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or <med>Postpartum Support International</med> (1-800-944-4773) for 24-hr support
4. Begin basic self-care: 20-min daily walks, balanced meals, accept help with night feeds to protect 4-hour sleep blocks
5. Discuss with provider the possibility of <med>evidence-based therapy</med> (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and/or <med>sertraline</med> or <med>escitalopram</med>, preferred <med>SSRIs</med> in breastfeeding
6. Schedule follow-up in 1 week to review symptom trajectory and treatment plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style interview (self-report + clinician queries)

Symptoms endorsed (≥ 7 days in past week unless noted):
- Marked anhedonia: minimal spontaneous laughter/pleasure; activities feel “forced” or chore-like  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, “heavy sadness”; crying spells without clear precipitant  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia linked to ruminating worries about infant safety  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt regarding infant care; cognitions of maternal inadequacy  
- Recurrent intrusive worries (SIDS, choking) and nocturnal panic episodes (tight chest, palpitations)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” difficulty completing routine tasks; identifies daily stressors  
- No self-harm ideation, intent, or plan endorsed (Q10 denied)

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, causing subjective distress and functional difficulty with infant care/household tasks; no current safety concerns.

Screening significance:  
Elevated risk for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety. Meets threshold for further evaluation (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS formal scoring) and possible referral to maternal mental health specialty services.

Next steps discussed: Review scoring, discuss referral options, provide psycho-education and crisis resources.
